newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe sees poverty breeding instability in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe sees poverty breeding instability in Africa.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe urged black Americans on Wednesday to help Africa achieve rapid economic progress, warning that slow growth would breed further political instability on the world's poorest continent.
Officially opening an African-American business summit, Mugabe also urged Africa to pursue a democratic path, saying any other way would promote conflict and suffering.
Africa's new struggle, he said, was to achieve rapid economic progress in order to uplift its poor.

"When people are hungry, ignorant, sickly and incapable of producing enough food for themselves, conflicts are invariably inevitable," he said to about 1,000 delegates who began meeting in Zimbabwe on Tuesday to discuss boosting trade, investment and economic aid from the United States to Africa.

"Such conflicts have begun to emerge in some African countries as people begin to exploit their God-given differences of race, ethnicity and languages in conjuction with man-made prejudices to get their uppper hand on others," he said.

The four-day African/African-American Summit is being attended by several African leaders and some top U.S. business executives in a large delegation led by civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater.
The conference has however been overshadowed by Mugabe's domestic problems.
Guerrilla war veterans staged a dramatic protest at the summit on Tuesday, demanding a meeting with Mugabe to resolve a dispute over war victims compensation.
They however retreated on Wednesday in the face of a government ban on demonstrations to prevent further embarrassment.

Home Affairs Minister Dumiso Dabengwa announced the ban on Tuesday night, saying it would last two weeks and affect "all demonstrations that disrupt the smooth flow of traffic and inconvenience the public".
The Zimbabwean president also urged Africa -- which is notorious for military coups -- to accelerate its democratisation programme to help achieve peace and sustainable economic growth.

"The time is over for the soldier-come-soldier-go system of government. We are therefore resolute in our determination to see the blossoming of sustainable democratic systems of governance on the continent," he said.

"Political reforms that have taken place and continue to do so are our surest guarantee of diffusing tension which often lead to internal and interstate armed and other conflicts that cause further division and suffering among us," he said to a loud cheer.
Mugabe assumed the chairmanship of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) for a year at a summit in Harare in June.
